## Four apps, four gnomAD clients

::: {.bignums}
::: {}
4

apps
:::

::: {}
3

gnomAD clients that disagreed
:::

::: {}
2

MyGene clients, one without batch
:::
:::

::: {.walls}
::: {.w1}
chunk size

25, 20, or unbounded
:::

::: {.w2}
a missing gene

NULL, NA row, or dropped
:::

::: {.w3}
service down

crash, NULL, or retry forever
:::

::: {.w4}
the trap

TTN resolved to TTR in two of them
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Same service, same author, three answers. That is not bad luck, that is a missing layer.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: The duplication was real, and the copies disagreed in ways that
changed results.

SCRIPT: Before this package, the family of apps had three gnomAD clients
and two MyGene clients. They disagreed about chunk sizes, about what a
missing gene looks like, and about what happens when the service is down.
Two of them quietly resolved TTN to TTR, because MyGene scores an alias of
the wrong gene above the exact match. That is the origin story: one client
per service, written once, with the traps written down.

NUMBERS: 3 gnomAD copies, 2 MyGene copies.

HONESTY: The apps are private. Say "in the family" and move on.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 0:50.

IF ASKED: "Why not use an existing CRAN client per service?" Most exist
for one service and return their own shape and their own error convention.
The point here is one shape.
:::

## Client half, parser half

![](../assets/diagrams/client-parser.svg){.nostretch width="92%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.payoff}
The parser is pure. The test suite runs without a network, and so can yours.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: Every module is two functions, and the pure half is the one you
test.

SCRIPT: Each service module is two halves. The client builds the request,
calls biohttp, hands the body to the parser, returns the envelope. It
touches the network. The parser takes an already parsed body and returns a
tibble or NULL. It never touches the network, which means it is tested
against a stored response body, and the whole suite runs offline.

NUMBERS: 2 halves per module.

HONESTY: Read fixtures with simplifyVector FALSE. The parsers expect the
nested list shape, not the data frames jsonlite guesses at.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 2:20.

IF ASKED: "How do you keep fixtures current?" A gated live test file runs
against the real services on demand and flags a shape change.
:::

## Nothing found is an answer

```r
mygene_gene("NOTAREALGENE123")$status
#> [1] "no_data"

mygene_gene("TP53")$status
#> [1] "ok"
```

::: {.cards}
::: {.teal}
`no_data`

The service was reached. It has nothing for this query. Show "not found".
:::

::: {.orange}
`error`, `timeout`

The service was not reached, or failed. Show "try again", not "not found".
:::

::: {}
`skipped`

We did not ask. The host is paused. Say so.
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
A UI that says "not found" during an outage is lying to the user.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: Distinguish "the service has nothing" from "the service is down",
because the UI must say different things.

SCRIPT: A symbol that resolves to nothing comes back no_data. The service
was reached and said so. When the service is down you get error or timeout,
and when the breaker is open you get skipped. The hand rolled client
returned NULL for all three, and the UI said not found during every outage.

NUMBERS: 3 statuses that used to be one NULL.

HONESTY: None.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 3:00.

IF ASKED: "Is no_data cached?" The transport response is, a 200 with an
empty body. The client turns it into no_data on every replay.
:::

## One row per input, in input order

```r
mygene_genes(c("TP53", "NOTAREALGENE123", "BRAF"))$data
#>   symbol           name                            entrez ensembl_gene
#>   TP53             tumor protein p53               7157   ENSG00000141510
#>   NOTAREALGENE123  NA                              NA     NA
#>   BRAF             B-Raf proto-oncogene            673    ENSG00000157764
```

::: {.walls .g2}
::: {.w3}
the contract

N inputs, N rows, same order. A miss is an NA row in place.
:::

::: {.w1}
what it prevents

A two row table shifts BRAF onto the second input. Every join after that is wrong.
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Every batch function in the package keeps this. Zip results onto your input by position.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: A batch never drops a row, because a shorter table silently
shifts everything after the gap.

SCRIPT: The batch functions are why the package is worth installing: three
symbols is one round trip. The contract is one row per input, in input
order. The middle row here is NA, not missing. A table with two rows would
have put BRAF on the second input and every join downstream would be wrong
without an error anywhere.

NUMBERS: 3 in, 3 out.

HONESTY: A failed chunk in a long list yields NA rows for that chunk, not
a failed call, unless every chunk failed.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 3:40.

IF ASKED: "Why not return only the hits and a list of misses?" Because
every caller then re-implements the join, and one of them gets it wrong.
:::

## Traps, written down

::: {.cards .c4}
::: {.orange}
TTN vs TTR

MyGene scores the alias higher. Exact symbol match wins.
:::

::: {.orange}
`HGNC` is upper case

Every other MyGene field is lower case. Asking for `hgnc` returns nothing.
:::

::: {.orange}
25 aliases

gnomAD's cost cap. Chunk at 20. Re-verified 2026-08-30.
:::

::: {.orange}
Reactome is a bare array

A parser reaching for a `results` key reports every gene as pathway free.
:::
:::

```r
# from R/mygene.R
#  "This is the single most important thing in this file."
mygene_pick_hit(hits, "TTN")$entrezgene
#> [1] "7273"
```

::: {.payoff}
Each trap has a comment with a date, and a test that pins it.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: The value of the package is as much the traps it remembers as
the requests it makes.

SCRIPT: Four of the traps. MyGene ranks an alias of the wrong gene above
the exact symbol, so the client prefers an exact match. MyGene names one
field HGNC in upper case and every other field lower case. gnomAD's limit
is a query cost, and the verified ceiling is 25 aliases, so the client
chunks at 20. Reactome answers with a bare array. Each of these is a comment
in the source with the date it was verified, and a test.

NUMBERS: 25 alias cap, chunk 20, verified 2026-08-30.

HONESTY: Quote the date. Limits change.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 4:30.

IF ASKED: "What about MyVariant?" Its default is hg19. The client asks
for hg38 explicitly. That is trap five.
:::

## Limits are hard coded where they were verified

```r
vep_default_throttle()
#> $capacity 1   $fill_time_s 1

bioclients:::clinvar_throttle()
#> $capacity 3   $fill_time_s 1        # 10 with NCBI_API_KEY

clinvar_classification(term)
# throttle = clinvar_throttle(), secret_query = list(api_key = NCBI_API_KEY)
```

::: {.flow}
::: {}
throttle

the service's documented rate, as the default
:::

::: {}
`secret_query`

the key attached at dispatch only
:::

::: {}
never in the cache key

never in a printed request
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
A caller who has not read the service docs still behaves.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: The rate limits and the credential handling are defaults, not
homework for the caller.

SCRIPT: NCBI allows three requests a second, ten with a key. VEP asks for
one. ClinGen was measured at three. Each client carries its own default.
The key itself goes through secret_query, which attaches it at dispatch, so
it is never part of the cache key and never appears in a printed request or
an error message.

NUMBERS: ClinVar 3/s or 10/s, VEP 1/s, ClinGen 3/s.

HONESTY: These are not called live in the talk. They are slow by design.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 5:10.

IF ASKED: "Can I override a throttle?" Yes, every client passes dots
through to biohttp. Pass throttle NULL at your own risk.
:::

## Chaining sources

```r
res <- mygene_gene("TP53")
uniprot_diseases(res$data$uniprot)$data
#>   name                    acronym mim     causal
#>   Li-Fraumeni syndrome    LFS     151623  TRUE
#>   ...

opentargets_gene_diseases(res$data$ensembl_gene, size = 3)
```

::: {.cards}
::: {}
Open Targets takes an Ensembl id

Resolve the symbol first. The client will not do it for you.
:::

::: {.teal}
on purpose

A client that silently calls a second service makes a MyGene outage look like an Open Targets outage.
:::

::: {.green}
`causal`

"caused by variants" versus "may be involved". Both arrive as disease comments.
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
One call, one service, one envelope. Composition happens in your code, where you can see it.
:::

::: notes
ONE JOB: Clients do not hide a second call to a different service, so a
failure always names the service that failed.

SCRIPT: Open Targets wants an Ensembl id, so you resolve the symbol through
MyGene first. The client does not do that for you, deliberately. If it did,
a MyGene outage would surface as an Open Targets failure and you would debug
the wrong service. The UniProt example shows a parser decision: causal is
read from the note text, because "caused by variants" and "may be involved"
are different claims that arrive in the same field.

NUMBERS: 2 calls, 2 envelopes.

HONESTY: None.

MEME: none.

CLOCK: leave by 5:50.

IF ASKED: "Why a Boolean for causal?" So a review can filter on it. The
note text is still in the tibble.
:::
